title: Social media reduction and well-being
description: Revisits major debates in research on social media and well-being. Tests whether the effects of reducing social media use on well-being differ by gender and age, and whether changes in social comparison, sleep, and body image help explain them.

title: Expectations and the effects of reducing social media use
description: Tests whether participants' expectations about what reducing social media use will do relate to the effects they actually experience. Also examines whether broader beliefs that social media harms well-being or democracy relate to the study's key outcomes.

title: Resilience to the polarizing effects of social media
description: Identifies the user characteristics and usage patterns that protect people from the polarizing and other negative effects of social media. Candidate factors include digital literacy and having a diverse online network alongside a less diverse offline one.

title: Social media and meta-perceptions of the outgroup
description: Tests whether reducing social media use weakens people's belief that members of opposing political and social groups dislike them. Builds on the idea that social media acts as a funhouse mirror that distorts how we see other groups.

title: Global Social Media Experiment data descriptor
description: Documents the full multi-country dataset, including how the data were collected and what was measured, so that other researchers can reuse it.

title: Social media reduction and information overload
description: Tests whether cutting back on social media reduces information overload: feeling overwhelmed by too much information and struggling to process it all.

title: Forecasting the effects of social media reduction
description: Surveys the general public, academics, and policy experts about what they expect the study's intervention to do, and compares their predictions across groups.

title: Power, status, and asymmetric polarization
description: Uses data collected before the intervention to test whether polarization is asymmetric, depending on which political and ethnic groups hold, or have historically held, more power and status.

title: Online political engagement and offline political action
description: Examines whether people who engage more with political posts online are less likely to take part in other forms of political action.

title: Culture and the effects of reducing social media use
description: Tests whether people's experiences of reducing social media use differ across cultures, comparing more individualist and more collectivist societies.

title: Participant reflections after the intervention
description: Collects qualitative follow-up data from participants about their experiences of reducing their social media use during the study.
